    p1.2  It flows 688 miles from its headwaters in the Appalachian foothills of eastern Kentucky, through northern Tennessee, and back into western Kentucky before joining the Ohio River.

    p2.1  Native American peoples including the Cherokee, Chickasaw, and Shawnee used the Cumberland for trade, travel, and settlement long before European contact.

    p2.3  French traders had earlier called it the Shawnee River.

    p3.1  Nashville's founding in 1779 by James Robertson and John Donelson was tied directly to the river.
    p3.2  Donelson led a flotilla of flatboats carrying families up the Cumberland to the site of Fort Nashborough in the winter of 1779 and 1780.
    p3.3  The settlement grew on the bluff above the river because the river was the only road.

    p4.1  Steamboats reached Nashville in 1819, and the river became the city's link to the cotton and tobacco markets of New Orleans.
    p4.2  By the 1850s Nashville was a major river port, and warehouses lined the waterfront.
    p4.3  Cotton, tobacco, iron, and lumber moved downriver; manufactured goods came back up.

    p5.1  The river also brought danger.
    p5.2  The flood of 1927 covered much of the low city.

    p6.2  Wolf Creek Dam, completed in 1951, created Lake Cumberland.
    p6.3  Old Hickory Dam, completed in 1954, created Old Hickory Lake just upstream of Nashville, and Cheatham Dam below the city regulates the river's level through downtown.

    p7.3  Cumberland Park, the pedestrian bridge, and the Ascend Amphitheater sit on the banks where the warehouses stood.

    p11.1  From there, the wider river, now named Cumberland, continues flowing west through the mountains of Kentucky before turning northward toward Cumberland Falls .

    p12.1  Nashville and the Cumberland As the Cumberland River winds its way through Tennessee, it serves as a defining feature of the state’s capital city, Nashville.
    p12.2  From its early days as a fledgling settlement to its emergence as a vibrant metropolis, Nashville’s destiny has been intertwined with the ebb and flow of the Cumberland.
    p12.3  The river provided a gateway for commerce and industry, fueling the city’s growth and prosperity.
    p12.4  Today, Nashville’s skyline is punctuated by the iconic bridges spanning the Cumberland, a testament to the enduring bond between urban development and natural beauty.

    p13.1  Cumberland River flowing through Nashville, Tennessee.
